sources.title: South African History Online: Afrikaner Bond
sources.note: Cape political context: British rule, representative government in 1853 and responsible government in 1872.

sources.title: South African History Online: Cape Town timeline
sources.note: British occupations, Batavian interlude and nineteenth-century city development.

sources.title: Iziko Museums: Excavation at the Slave Lodge
sources.note: Gabeba Abrahams-Willis describes 2000 excavation and preliminary findings. Layers span several centuries; food and small finds are not all securely dated to 1800.

sources.title: Iziko Museums: Koopmans-de Wet House
sources.note: Room descriptions distinguish reconstructed furnishings, donated objects and documented features. Imagined scenes are not used as eyewitness evidence.

sources.title: Iziko Museums: End of enslavement
sources.note: Cape emancipation on 1 December 1834 followed by compulsory apprenticeship until December 1838. Use Cape dates only.

sources.title: South African History Online: Eastern Cape Wars of Dispossession
sources.note: Nine frontier wars and dispossession from 1779 to 1878; communities and land, not simply a changing border.

sources.title: New York Public Library: Imvo zabantsundu
sources.note: Catalogue records John Tengo Jabavu, King William’s Town, first issue 3 November 1884, Xhosa and English, English section Native opinion.

sources.title: South African Astronomical Observatory: History
sources.note: Institutional history of the 1820 observatory, Fallows’s temporary hut and 1824 catalogue, and nineteenth-century time signals.

sources.title: The Presidency of South Africa: History
sources.note: Union on 31 May 1910 and exclusion of Black South Africans from constitutional negotiations.

sources.title: South African History Online: Indian South Africans timeline, 1654 to 1899
sources.note: Natal annexation and separate colonial charter; arrival of Truro in 1860; Bauboo Naidoo’s 1861 food shop.

sources.title: South African History Online: Indian indentured labour in Natal, 1860 to 1911
sources.note: Recruitment, surviving ship records and end of recruitment in 1911.

sources.title: Jo Beall: Women under indentured labour in colonial Natal, 1860 to 1911
sources.note: Research chapter in Women and Gender in Southern Africa to 1945; estate work, tea plucking, household and garden labour.

sources.title: South African History Online: Anglo-Zulu wars
sources.note: British ultimatum, 1879 war and later annexations. Natal and the Zulu kingdom are distinct institutions.

sources.title: Ohlange High School Development Trust: History
sources.note: Institutional account credits John and Nokutela Dube with establishing Ohlange in 1901; indexed text accessible, rendered page text empty.

sources.title: National Library of South Africa: Ilanga lase Natal digital collection
sources.note: Indexed collection description names John Dube, Ohlange, April 1903. Dynamic viewer requires JavaScript; title verified in institutional index.

sources.title: Stellenbosch University ESAT: Ilanga lase Natal
sources.note: Title translation The Natal Sun. Avoid disputed priority claim and conflicting founding-month detail.

sources.title: Phoenix Settlement: About
sources.note: Community institution’s account of 1904 land purchase, relocated printing press, food gardens and support for campaigners’ families.

sources.title: South African History Online: Union of South Africa inaugurated
sources.note: 31 May 1910 union of Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies.

sources.title: South African Military History Society: Die stryd tussen Boer en Brit in Transvaal, 1877 to 1881
sources.note: Historical article on British annexation and the war restoring republican government; used for basic chronology.

sources.title: Gauteng City-Region Observatory: Mining landscapes of the Gauteng City-Region
sources.note: Research account of the 1886 goldfields, migration, labour, industrial development and environmental legacy.

sources.title: Ditsong Museums: Kruger Museum
sources.note: 1884 house, railway coach and adjacent pass-office site; avoid the page’s typographical 1889 to 1881 war date.

sources.title: Ditsong Museums: Pioneer Museum
sources.note: 1848 clay house, earthen floors, thatch and reconstructed nineteenth-century rural furnishings and garden.

sources.title: Ditsong Museums: Sammy Marks Museum
sources.note: House collection with 98 percent of contents attributed to the Marks family; museum interpretation, not a typical household.

sources.title: Jaco Schoonraad, Ditsong Museums: Centenary of the demise of Sammy Marks
sources.note: Curator’s account of coal, distillery, glass and preserve enterprises; Zwartkoppies building and family history.

sources.title: Elaine Katz: The white death, silicosis on the Witwatersrand gold mines, 1886 to 1910
sources.note: Wits doctoral research: dust disease and unsupported claims that short African labour contracts protected workers.

sources.title: University of Pretoria Library: De Volksstem historical photograph and caption
sources.note: Caption gives title and first issue 8 August 1873; photograph shows later 1930s premises. Only historical newspaper title is quoted.

sources.title: National Army Museum: Boer War
sources.note: Campaign, African and Indian participants, scorched earth and concentration camps, Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902. Shared word budget across two cards.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Postal Museum: South Africa
sources.note: Former colonies’ postal and constitutional transformations. Use Transvaal and Orange Free State entries only; no use of disputed Zululand date.

sources.title: South African History Online: The struggle over land, the Basotho lose out
sources.note: Bloemfontein Convention, exclusion of African chiefdoms and contested boundaries; land losses.

sources.title: National Museum: First Raadsaal Museum
sources.note: 1849 building used as school, church, council chamber and museum; restored building distinguished from untouched interior.

sources.title: National Museum Annual Report, 2019 to 2020: Freshford House
sources.note: Freshford completed 1897, architect John Edwin Harrison; red brick, bay windows, veranda and metalwork.

sources.title: Mariaana Botes, National Museum: Water pure and wholesome
sources.note: Historian’s account of bucket transport, water shortages and Modder River scheme supplying town in 1899. Does not prove universal household connection.

sources.title: National Museum: Wagon Museum
sources.note: Collection of ox wagons, stagecoaches, carts and transport exhibits; not all local-provenance originals.

sources.title: National Museum: Culna 77, How did an ox-wagon brake?
sources.note: Skidpan chains placed under rear wheels, traditional wagons before later brake mechanisms; labeled earlier transport context.

sources.title: National Museum: Black people and passbooks in republican Bloemfontein
sources.note: Original historical research quotes Law No. 8 of 1893 and contemporary press on raids. Exact Dutch phrase verblijf brief and translation residential pass.

sources.title: National Museum: The National Museum, 1877 to 1915
sources.note: Foundation, first curator Exton, government support, 1884 caretaker and expansion.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: Namibia, Deutschland exhibition introduction
sources.note: German colonial rule 1884 to 1915; 1904 to 1908 war and genocide, and continuing communities of memory.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: Mission und koloniale Begegnung
sources.note: Oorlam, Nama, Herero cattle society, missionaries, traders, treaties and growing settler presence in the 1890s.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: Windhoek, Leben in der Stadt
sources.note: 1891 administration and German segregation; 1959 forced removals and surviving letter-marked doors under apartheid. Shared with modern Namibia.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: Widerstand, Krieg, Völkermord
sources.note: 1904 conflict, deliberate expulsion into Omaheke, Nama resistance and camps until 1908.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World: Letter journals of Hendrik Witbooi
sources.note: Witbooi’s African political analysis and attempts to form a united front against colonial treaties; registered 2005.

sources.title: Hendrik Witbooi: Letter No. 3, 13 October 1885, DBNL edition
sources.note: 1929 printed edition, page 12, transcribes letter to Maharero. Historical Dutch spelling preserved; quote Ik ben Uwen Vriend.

sources.title: Samuel Maharero: Letter to Hendrik Witbooi, 1 November 1892, DBNL edition
sources.note: Incoming letter in Witbooi papers, 1929 edition pages 187 to 189. Correct attribution is Maharero, not Witbooi. Settlement, peace negotiations and greeting to wife and children.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: Citizenships exhibition booklet, 2022
sources.note: Page 13 exhibits a 1907 Swakopmund metal pass marker, numbered 8035; use physical object as material evidence of administrative classification.

sources.title: Liina Kaunapawa Nambahu, Museums Association of Namibia: Museum Matters 37
sources.note: Youth review of TransNamib Museum, page 59, criticizes display neglect of forced African railway labour. Avoid incorrect approximate rinderpest date in review.

sources.title: Charmaine Tjizezenga, Museums Association of Namibia: Museum Matters 28
sources.note: Page 29: 32 Finnish missionary photographs in Nakambale display, oldest from 1893; subjects include King Kambonde, his wife and a missionary’s wife.

sources.title: Museums Association of Namibia: First World War teachers’ guide
sources.note: Drivers and Labourers section; photographs NAN 5657 and 5689 show Black railway workers and supply unloading during 1915 campaign.

sources.title: Eric Moore Ritchie: With Botha in the Field, 1915
sources.note: Contemporary campaign narrative reproduces surrender terms signed on 9 July 1915. Partisan account used for the dated document, not neutral social history.

sources.title: United Nations in Namibia: The UN’s role in Namibian independence
sources.note: 1946 petitions, UN Institute for Namibia, 1989 election and independence 21 March 1990.

sources.title: United Nations Peacekeeping: UNTAG summary
sources.note: Termination of South African mandate in 1966, mobile voter registration in 1989, constitution and independence.

sources.title: International Water Association: Potable water reuse, opportunities and challenges
sources.note: Windhoek started direct potable reuse in 1968; technical case-study programme.

sources.title: International Water Association: Global Trends, 2022
sources.note: Water reclamation section: old and new Goreangab plants; new plant from 2002 uses multiple barriers and blends treated water.

sources.title: UNICEF Namibia: Making handwashing with soap a habit at school
sources.note: 29 September 2017, Onakatumbe Combined School; stations near classrooms and toilets, routines before food.

sources.title: UNICEF Namibia: Water delivery brings relief to thirsty learners
sources.note: 28 February 2018, King Kauluma Combined School: borehole breakdown, meal and flush-toilet interruption, tanker delivery.

sources.title: UNESCO: Marula festivals in southern Africa, case study
sources.note: Namibian festival: carving, fruit gathering, fermentation and transmission through shared work. Contemporary practices, not undated ancient customs.

sources.title: UNESCO: Aixan ancestral musical sound knowledge and skills assistance
sources.note: 2018 to 2019 project describes Nama and Damara performance at weddings, rainy-season celebrations and education.

sources.title: Permanent Mission of Namibia to the UN: Constitution, Chapter 1
sources.note: Article 1(6), exact English sentence. Institutional indexed text checked; direct fetch returned internal error.

sources.title: Uukwambi Traditional Authority: Consent for Oshituthi shomagongo nomination, 2013
sources.note: Dated 5 November 2013, bilingual consent letter headed Omukanda gwepitikilo (Certificate of Consent); eight northern traditional authorities.

sources.title: John Iliffe: Review of Jan Vansina, Antecedents to Modern Rwanda
sources.note: English Historical Review 121 (2006), pages 649 to 650. Scholarly discussion of oral evidence, expanding kingdom and political change; no fixed uncontested founding year asserted.

sources.title: Michał Tymowski: A five-day week in Rwanda
sources.note: Social Evolution and History 22 (2023). Publishes and analyzes Jan Czekanowski’s 1907 diary; regional variation and disagreement about introduction of labour obligations remain explicit.

sources.title: Claudine Vidal: Économie de la société féodale rwandaise
sources.note: Cahiers d’études africaines 14 (1974), pages 52 to 74; page 52 describes crops, hoes, manure, fallow, household enclosures and famine. Scope is central, southern and western regions under longstanding state control.

sources.title: Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy: Museums and heritage sites
sources.note: Palace replica and twentieth-century building distinguished; Inyambo display introduced in 2011. Museum page dates modern palace 1931; avoid conflicting 1932 date elsewhere.

sources.title: British Museum: Basket Af1921,0512.10
sources.note: Coiled grass basket, 1921 or shortly before, Rwanda; register specifies millet stalks, papyrus leaf and soot, used to hold a chief’s beer calabash. Later witness, not a nineteenth-century excavation.

sources.title: Eugène Hurel, Tales, Fables and Narratives of Rwanda, 2023 scholarly edition
sources.note: Brack, Sibomana and Doldo edit tales collected in 1908 to 1919 and published in 1922. Preface states modernization of spelling, tone and vowel length. Tale 13 paragraph 2 supplies short sample and translation on pages 12 to 13.

sources.title: Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy: Igazeti Umurage, number 3
sources.note: 2022 journal, page 97, early missionary writing and Hurel’s 1911 manual and Dufays dictionary. Do not infer universal literacy.

sources.title: NYU GlobaLex: Rwanda’s legal system and legal materials
sources.note: Legal scholars describe German then Belgian colonial administration, monarchy’s decline, republic and independence.

sources.title: National Electoral Commission of Rwanda: Twenty years
sources.note: Historical section records 1961 referendum and anti-Tutsi violence; institutional perspective kept distinct from endorsement of every interpretation.

sources.title: UN General Assembly: The future of Ruanda-Urundi, Resolution 1746
sources.note: 27 June 1962 resolution, paragraph 2: trusteeship ends 1 July and Rwanda and Burundi become separate sovereign states.

sources.title: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda: The genocide
sources.note: Official tribunal history of 1994 crimes, chiefly against Tutsi civilians and also moderate Hutu; non-graphic summary.

sources.title: British Museum: Anklet Af1948,08.157
sources.note: Grass-plaited anklet from Ruhondo village, Ruhengeri district, circa 1947, collected by John Lister; register says worn by women in sets.

sources.title: Parliament of Rwanda: Constitution, Official Gazette, 4 August 2023
sources.note: Printed page 24, opening of preamble: Twebwe, Abanyarwanda; aligned official English We, the People of Rwanda.

sources.title: WHO Africa: Community health workers lead the fight against malaria in Rwanda
sources.note: 25 April 2023, Esther Urimubenshi and community worker Theoneste Nezehose, supplies and referral support from Mayange Health Centre.

sources.title: UNICEF Rwanda: SATO, more than just pans and taps
sources.note: 2023 reporting and photographs; Jean Baptiste Mbonyeyezu’s early-childhood centre, weighted pan seal and handwashing. Promotional impact anecdotes not treated as clinical evaluation.

sources.title: Rwanda Biomedical Centre: Medical drone deliveries press release, 14 October 2016
sources.note: Muhanga launch; initial purpose reducing delivery time and waste of perishable blood products. Capacity targets are not reported as measured accomplishments.

sources.title: Azizi Life: Our purpose
sources.note: Rwandan artisan partner organization reports women sharing farming and child-rearing knowledge during cooperative work; own account of activities, not national statistics.

sources.title: Emma Lawson, Azizi Life: Arts and crafts at the Azizi Life Studio
sources.note: 14 June 2018 interview with Chantal; Dove Montessori students and artisan Alex making imigongo designs.

batchIdentityNotes.note: All imported records end in 1914, but the colonies joined the Union on 31 May 1910. Transvaal crosses 1877 to 1881 British rule, restored republic, war and later British colony. Orange Free State annexation was proclaimed in 1900; war and final surrender continued until 1902. No shared card or geometry substitution proposed.

German record spans 1914 to 1920 but actual German rule ended July 1915. Namibia record starts 1945 during South African rule, not independence; independence was 21 March 1990. Separate narratives retain these distinctions.

Decoded 1815 feature bounds [26.649,-6.014,32.521,-2.463] are misplaced south of Rwanda. The 1878, 1880 and 1900 features have Rwanda bounds [29.482,-2.711,31.185,-1.109]. Do not use 1815 geometry as evidence of kingdom extent. Imported 1914 endpoint is not abolition of monarchy, which occurred in 1961.
1945 modern record covers Belgian administration followed by 1962 independence; bounds [28.806,-2.921,30.89,-1.154]. No merging with kingdom card.
